channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: The Gadget That's Better in Crowds Than Your Phone + Ring’s Founder Before Amazon Bought It | E2349
gist: The first ~35 min is a Totem Labs interview: founder Carter Fowler pitches an offline mesh-network compass that gets better with crowd density (Lost Lands: 10%+ penetration, 330k offline messages, ~58% gross margin after repricing from $49 to $88) and argues data-generating hardware is a rare moat as AI commoditizes SaaS. The remainder is a 2017 archive retrospective of Ring founder Jamie Siminoff (not discussed with Fowler), covering mission focus as 'cheating', betting on friends, IPO-vs-sale, and how Flock-style surveillance hit a privacy backlash.

themes.theme: Totem mesh network: congestion as the unsolved connectivity problem

insights.claim: Totem Labs argues every major mass gathering (festivals like EDC, Lost Lands, even CES) is a failure condition for cellular networks, so it built an offline autonomous mesh network (Unity Mesh) that keeps groups connected without towers.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Crowd-density connectivity is a real, recurring failure mode that incumbents' architecture does not solve.
insights.quote: every major gathering is basically a failure condition for conventional connectivity networks

insights.claim: Totem's mesh scales inversely to cellular: each additional device acts as a relay for strangers' messages, so performance improves with density while phones degrade.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: A hardware product with built-in positive network effects in exactly the environments where incumbents fail.
insights.quote: The more cell phones you get in an area, the worse they all work. The more totems you get in an area, the better they all work.

insights.claim: At Lost Lands (~50,000 attendees) Totem reached over 10% penetration (5,000+ users), recording 35 hops across the festival, over 330,000 messages in a weekend and offline connections spanning over 1.5 km.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Concrete proof the mesh works at scale once density passes ~10% at a single dense event.

insights.claim: Mesh networks have an inherent cold-start problem akin to a two-sided marketplace; at ~1% penetration the network still works but may not provide full connectivity at distance.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Adoption density per venue, not total units, is the key KPI for any mesh-network business.

insights.claim: Totem claims median positioning accuracy of about one meter using multi-constellation GNSS, 5-15x better than phones in crowds, where phone GPS drift ranges 20-150 ft.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Precision positioning in crowds is a differentiated technical claim and the basis for its data moat.
insights.quote: GPS drift with phones can be anywhere from 20 feet to 150 ft.

insights.claim: The device stack is three layers: multi-constellation GNSS, a 2.4 GHz peer-to-peer protocol enabling second-by-second updates, and the Unity Mesh relay network.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Real-time update cadence matters because a minute of lag in a dense crowd puts hundreds of people between friends.

insights.claim: Phones position poorly in crowds because they blend GPS with cell-tower trilateration and nearby-device sensing (e.g., Apple's Find My), all designed around an assumption of constant connectivity.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Explains why congestion degrades phone location exactly when it is needed most.

insights.claim: Apple, Samsung and similar incumbents are unlikely to ship offline decentralized mesh features because it would undercut their always-connected model and antagonize carriers that subsidize tens of millions of phones a year.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Innovator's-dilemma protection for offline-connectivity startups: the obvious competitor is structurally disincentivized.
insights.quote: large companies like Apple, Samsung, any of these rarely ship products or technology that undercut their core business model

insights.claim: Fowler argues the last big unsolved problem in connectivity is no longer coverage (largely solved by players like Starlink) but congestion.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Points investors toward congestion/density solutions rather than more coverage plays.
insights.quote: the real last frontier big unsolved problem with connectivity is not coverage anymore. It is congestion.

themes.theme: Hardware unit economics and network-effect pricing

insights.claim: Totem launched the compass at $49 each ($37 at 5+ units, roughly cost) to seed network density, and now sells it for about $88 as the network has become more valuable.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Network-effect hardware can underprice early to solve cold start, then reprice up as utility compounds.

insights.claim: Totem reports its best-ever gross margin of around 58% over the last month or two, which it calls healthy for a hardware company.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Margin expansion from repricing, not cost cuts, validates the network-value pricing thesis.

insights.claim: Average purchase group size rose from about 2.6-2.7 units early on to about 3.8-3.9 now, making the four-pack (around $365) the most popular package.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Group-based purchasing is native virality and raises order value.

insights.claim: About 30% of Totem purchases in recent months cited a recommendation or seeing someone wearing the glowing device at an event, making the product a native advertisement for itself.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Low-CAC visible-hardware loop; combined with ~800M social views it suggests organic distribution.

insights.claim: Totem raised about $1.3M in a pre-seed round and $1.6M via crowdfunding, more from customers than from VCs, which host Alex Wilhelm framed as strong product-market-fit evidence.
insights.speaker: Alex Wilhelm
insights.so_what: Customer-funded hardware reduces dilution and signals demand before institutional capital.

insights.claim: Totem refuses to put the core device behind a subscription (buy once, own for life), planning optional premium consumer subscriptions and other revenue streams instead.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Revenue model is hardware-first; recurring revenue must come from data products, rentals and add-ons.

insights.claim: Totem plans on-site rentals at venues (around $30-40 per weekend, $15-20 per day, aimed at e.g. families at Disneyland and sports arenas), with a first pilot around New Year's Eve.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Rentals could expand TAM well beyond frequent festival-goers and seed density at new venue types.

insights.claim: Totem says it has generated around 800 million views across social media over two years.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Organic social reach is a key part of its consumer-hardware distribution.

themes.theme: Proprietary data as the moat after AI commoditizes software

insights.claim: Investor appetite shifted from B2B SaaS only (2024) to AI-in-the-tagline only (2025) to, in 2026, openness to hardware as investors realize AI value capture is uncertain and concentrated at the top.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: A real-time read of VC sentiment rotation toward hardware and non-AI-wrapper businesses.
insights.quote: people realize that the value distribution in AI is actually pretty uncertain and it seems pretty concentrated toward the top

insights.claim: Hardware that generates proprietary data is increasingly seen as one of the only remaining moats in a world where any SaaS product can be rebuilt overnight.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Bearish for software IP defensibility; bullish for data-generating physical products.
insights.quote: hardware that generates proprietary data is like kind of what some people look as really the only remaining moes in a world where pretty much any SAS product could be rebuilt overnight

insights.claim: Wilhelm argues that people decompiling apps to get to source code will crush software IP permanently.
insights.speaker: Alex Wilhelm
insights.so_what: Software defensibility erodes further; moats shift to data, distribution and atoms.

insights.claim: Totem is building a predictive crowd-flow simulation model from its anonymized, meter-level, second-by-second network data so organizers, security and sponsors can test layouts (exits, stages, kiosks) before gates open; pilot targeted in 3-4 months.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: B2B data product layered on consumer hardware could be the recurring-revenue engine; live events have a one-shot, year-long feedback loop.
insights.quote: watch their weekend unfold before the gates open

insights.claim: Fowler cites loneliness data (3% of Americans reported no close friends in 1990 vs 10% last year) alongside record ticket sales at Live Nation as evidence of strong demand for in-person experiences.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Supports a secular tailwind for live events and products around them.

themes.theme: Expansion beyond festivals: kids, accessibility, infrastructure independence, defense

insights.claim: Families with kids under 12 are Totem's second-largest customer segment, used as a screen-free alternative before giving children phones; one customer said it beat $500 Apple Watch Ultras he had tried.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: A sizable non-festival market for screen-free child locators and kid-safe offline messaging.

insights.claim: Totem has found adoption with ski patrol teams in Colorado and in blind and deaf communities, because many low-vision people can see lights but not faces beyond a few feet.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Unexpected accessibility and professional use cases broaden the TAM.

insights.claim: Totem's roadmap targets full infrastructure independence: offline texting and social networking over the mesh, a smaller haptic kids' 'buddy band', satellite-free dynamic trilateration within the mesh, and solar charging.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Moves the product from festival accessory toward a self-sustaining comms platform.

insights.claim: Fowler believes decentralized networks are the future for civilian and military use, citing Russian GNSS jamming in Ukraine and the Starlink shutoff as evidence of centralized-network fragility.
insights.speaker: Carter Fowler (Totem Labs)
insights.so_what: Decentralized mesh comms have dual-use/defense relevance where centralized links can be jammed or switched off.
insights.quote: That's the danger of a centralized network. There's actually a switch that can be flipped.

themes.theme: Ring founder lessons: tinkering, mission focus, friends as bets

insights.claim: Before Ring, Jamie Siminoff's PhoneTag (human-transcribed voicemail) sold to Nuance for little, and Unsubscribe.com was a beloved product nobody would pay for; it was sold and investors got their money back.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Users loving a product in tests does not mean they will pay; willingness to pay is the real signal.
insights.quote: the statistics can show you that they love the product but then in the final moment the credit card doesn't come out

insights.claim: Ring originated as a personal garage incubator where Siminoff built a Wi-Fi doorbell for himself because none existed; visitors immediately asked to buy it.
insights.speaker: Jamie Siminoff (Ring founder)
insights.so_what: Founder-need-driven invention plus spontaneous demand is a strong early signal.

insights.claim: Siminoff says a strong mission is 'cheating' because it eliminates distraction: Ring's 'reducing crime in neighborhoods' let staff reject adjacent ideas (e.g., a connected pet feeder) unless they made homes safer.
insights.speaker: Jamie Siminoff (Ring founder)
insights.so_what: A crisp mission acts as a product filter that prevents costly side quests.
insights.quote: having a strong mission is cheating

insights.claim: Lon Harris and Alex Wilhelm cite OpenAI's Sora consumer feed and browser as mission-creep examples, arguing Anthropic's Claude Code success forced OpenAI to refocus, and Sam Altman is now tightening OpenAI's narrative.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Focus is a competitive variable even for frontier labs; distractions show up as lost share.

insights.claim: Calacanis's angel lesson: always bet on friends with multiple small/medium exits, because you already know whether they will refuse to let the company die; a friend who backed out of Ring's ~$4M angel round missed what was described as a 50-100x.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Longitudinal knowledge of a founder's grit is a real information edge for angels.
insights.quote: You just always bet on your friends.

insights.claim: In 2017 Siminoff said his goal was to take Ring public rather than sell, arguing an acquirer would cut long-horizon spending like budgeting $5M on products launching in two years; Amazon bought Ring about a year later.
insights.speaker: Jamie Siminoff (Ring founder)
insights.so_what: Founder IPO intentions are weak predictors; strategic acquirers with distribution often win.

insights.claim: The hosts frame Amazon's Ring acquisition as verticalizing the front-door delivery loop and speculate Ring could provide the view for Prime Air drone drops.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Ring may be strategic infrastructure for Amazon last-mile logistics, not just a security product.

insights.claim: Hosts note Flock's license-plate-reader cameras faced public backlash, people attacking cameras with bats, and very public layoffs, showing that a single-minded safety mission without privacy limits hits a ceiling.
insights.speaker: Alex Wilhelm
insights.so_what: Surveillance-tech growth is constrained by social license; privacy backlash is a material business risk.
insights.quote: We don't want Minority Report. We want safe houses.

themes.theme: Startup ecosystem shifts: events, speed, scrutiny

insights.claim: Hosts argue CES lost its central role because big tech companies became 'nation states' with their own launch stages, and the AI focus on models and agents does not translate to gadget shows; robots may revive it.
insights.speaker: Alex Wilhelm
insights.so_what: Trade-show relevance tracks hardware cycles; a robotics wave could restore CES's importance.
insights.quote: Now tech companies are essentially nation states.

insights.claim: Hosts say startups now face instant scrutiny but also instant scale, citing an AI product reportedly out about three weeks that already has competitors, raised at a $7.5B valuation and is used by 30% of the Fortune 500 (caption names it 'Jev').
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Compressed timelines reduce room for quiet tinkering but raise upside; product name in captions is unclear.
